messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 7300, E 4100 is [4100, 7300]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-15, 15]}, visible_on: 'P-202'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'BASE:RTE-7', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('86+50@15R', 'PC-2'; BC-2 and EC-2 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('82+00@15R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
MAIN ST (alignment MAIN-ST, running east) and CROSS AVE (alignment CROSS-AVE, running north) cross at MAIN-ST 18+00 / CROSS-AVE 27+00. Their curb faces are drawn on rd_EP: MAIN ST's 44 ft either side of its centerline, CROSS AVE's 32 ft either side. Three corners have their curb returns; the northeast corner does not -- its two curb lines still run to meet at the corner. Draw the northeast curb return on rd_EP, a 50 ft radius arc tangent to both curb faces, and trim both curb lines back to where the return meets them.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

messages.content:
I've grasped the overall picture. The model backs up the task description:

- **MAIN-ST** centerline: y=5000 (running eastward), **CROSS-AVE** centerline: x=5000 (running northward) → intersection at [5000, 5000].
- Curb faces on rd_EP: MAIN ST y=5044 (north) / y=4956 (south); CROSS AVE x=5032 (east) / x=4968 (west).
- The three existing R=50 returns are the SE (AR-001), SW (AR-002), and NW (AR-003) arcs. The **NE corner** has none — the east curb of MAIN ST, **LN-003** ((5032,5044)→(5800,5044)), and the north curb of CROSS AVE, **LN-004** ((5032,5044)→(5032,5700)), meet at the corner point (5032, 5044).

A radius-50 fillet at this 90° corner becomes an arc with center at (5032+50, 5044+50) = (5082, 5094), with tangent points (5082, 5044) on LN-003 and (5032, 5094) on LN-004 — exactly the missing quadrant of the existing pattern. Both lines extend outward from the corner, so the fillet's default "keep" side is correct. The fillet both draws the tangent arc and trims the two curb lines back to the tangent points.
messages.reasoning:
Let's understand the geometry:

- MAIN-ST: alignment running east, centerline y=5000, from x=4200 to x=5800. Station 0+00 at x=4200 (station 18+00 = x=5000). Let's confirm: LN-001's anchor says station 1000.0... hmm, it says station 1000.0, offset 0.0, ref T-1. The start point of LN-001 is [4200, 5000]. Hmm, maybe the anchor station is 1000? No wait, MAIN-ST's station 18+00 is the intersection point. Let's confirm: CROSS-AVE runs north, centerline x=5000, from y=4300 to y=5700.

Actually the anchor says station 1000.0 for LN-001 (MAIN-ST T-1) and station 2000.0 for LN-002 (CROSS-AVE T-1). Hmm, that's odd. Maybe the begin station of the alignment isn't 0. Let's verify with get_design_data / list_alignments.

In any case, the task says the intersection is at MAIN-ST 18+00 / CROSS-AVE 27+00. In model coordinates that's the point [5000, 5000]. Let's confirm with station_to_xy for MAIN-ST station 18+00 and CROSS-AVE station 27+00.

Curb faces on rd_EP:
- MAIN ST's 44 feet: the north-side curb face y=5044 (offset -44 = left side; MAIN runs east so left is north): LN-003 (5032,5044) to (5800,5044) — the east portion; LN-009 (4200,5044) to (4918,5044) — the west portion. The south-side curb face y=4956 (offset +44 = right side): LN-005 (5082,4956) to (5800,4956); LN-007 (4200,4956) to (4918,4956).
- CROSS AVE's 32 feet: east-side curb face x=5032 (offset +32 = right; CROSS-AVE runs north so right is east): LN-004 (5032,5044) to (5032,5700) — north portion; LN-006 (5032,4300) to (5032,4906) — south portion. West-side curb face x=4968 (offset -32 = left): LN-008 (4968,4300) to (4968,4906); LN-010 (4968,5094) to (4968,5700).

Existing curb returns (R=50):
- AR-001: center (5082,4906) — SE corner? Let's see. The center is at the intersection of the south-side curb face y=4956? No wait, center (5082, 4906), radius 50. It's tangent to the east-side curb face x=5032? Distance from center to line x=5032 is 5082-5032 = 50. Yes. Tangent to the south-side curb face y=4956: distance 4956-4906 = 50. Yes. So the SE corner return, spanning angles 90° to 180°: the point at 90° = (5082, 4956) on the south curb face, the point at 180° = (5032, 4906) on the east curb face.
- AR-002: center (4918, 4906), 0° to 90°: point at 0° = (4968, 4906) on the west curb face, point at 90° = (4918, 4956) on the south curb face. SW corner.
- AR-003: center (4918, 5094), 270° to 0°: point at 270° = (4918, 5044) on the north curb face, point at 0° = (4968, 5094) on the west curb face. NW corner.

The NE corner (no return): the north-side curb face LN-003 (y=5044) and the east-side curb face LN-004 (x=5032) still run to the corner: LN-003 starts at (5032, 5044) and LN-004 starts at (5032, 5044). They meet at that corner point.

So the NE curb return: an arc of radius 50 tangent to both y=5044 (tangent at (5082, 5044)) and x=5032 (tangent at (5032, 5094)). Center = (5082, 5094). Arc from 180° to 270° (or from 270° CCW to 360°… let me think). The corner is at (5032, 5044). The arc center is at (5082, 5094) (inward, southeast of the corner: x+50, y+50). The tangent point on the east-side curb face x=5032 is (5032, 5094) — angle 180° from center. The tangent point on the north-side curb face y=5044 is (5082, 5044) — angle 270° from center. The arc runs from 180° CCW to 270° (passing through 225° = (5082-35.355, 5094-35.355) = (5046.64, 5058.64)). That's the corner cutout.

So: draw_arc center [5082, 5094], radius 50, start_angle 180, end_angle 270. (CCW from 180 to 270 — yes, that's a quarter circle through the third quadrant, i.e., the corner region.)

Then trim:
- LN-003 (the east-side north curb face, y=5044 from (5032,5044) to (5800,5044)): trim back to the tangent point (5082,5044). The portion to remove is the part near (5032,5044), i.e., the part between the corner and the tangent point. With the trim tool: targets [{id: LN-003, at: a point on the part to be removed}], with the boundaries including the arc. The arc crosses y=5044 at the tangent point (5082,5044). So the part to remove is the segment from (5032,5044) to (5082,5044); pick a point on that part, e.g., midpoint (5057, 5044).
- LN-004 (the north-side east curb face, x=5032 from (5032,5044) to (5032,5700)): trim to the tangent point (5032,5094). The part to remove is from (5032,5044) to (5032,5094); pick a point like (5032, 5069).

Boundaries: the arc (AR-… the new id), and maybe also the other curb lines. The arc's tangent point: for LN-003, the cutting edge is where the arc intersects y=5044 → x=5082. Good. For LN-004, the arc intersects x=5032 at y=5094. Good.

Actually, with trim, the boundaries default to all lines, polylines, arcs, circles in the space (references included). If I don't specify boundaries, every line becomes a cutting edge. That's fine — the part to remove on LN-003 is cut at the first intersection going left from the "at" point. The "at" point (5057,5044) is on the portion to be removed. Cutting edges crossing LN-003: the arc at (5082,5044) (tangent — hmm, the arc is tangent to y=5044, so does the arc "cross" it? The arc touches the line at exactly one point, the tangent point. Does the trim treat tangency as an intersection? A tangent arc touches the line at exactly one point, (5082,5044). The intersection should exist at that point. It should work, but tangency might be numerically tricky. Alternative: use break_entity on LN-003 with at = (5082,5044), or trim with the arc as the boundary.

Actually, the safest, most robust approach: trim with the arc specified as the boundary. If tangency isn't detected, I can fall back to trim with extend_boundaries, or directly use break_entity/lengthen with a computed point.

Alternatively, compute the tangent point myself (simple: center (5082,5094), tangent points (5082,5044) and (5032,5094)) and use break_entity at those points: split LN-003 at (5082,5044), delete the short piece (5032→5082). Similarly split LN-004 at (5032,5094) and delete the short piece. But the task says "trim both curb lines back to the point where the return meets them" — the trim tool is the natural method, and it preserves the anchors ("design linework retains its anchors, re-stationing"). If I break/delete, the anchored offset lines might lose their anchors. Trim "re-stations" anchored lines — better. Let's use trim with the arc as the boundary.

Plan:
1. fillet LN-003 and LN-004 with radius 50? The fillet tool: "rounds the corner between two lines with a curve of the given radius, tangent to both, and trims or extends the lines to meet it." The two lines meet exactly at (5032,5044). Fillet with radius 50 does everything: draw the arc + trim the lines. The tangent point is determined by the intersection. Since the corner is a 90° angle, the fillet is exactly the arc I described, center (5082,5094), tangent points (5082,5044) and (5032,5094).

However, the fillet's `keep` parameter: "when the lines cross, a point on the part of each line to keep; default: the ends of each line farther from the intersection." LN-003 starts at (5032,5044) [the corner] and ends at (5800,5044). The far end from the corner is (5800,5044) — keep it. LN-004 goes from (5032,5044) to (5032,5700); the far end is (5032,5700). The defaults work perfectly.

The fillet's layer: "the layer of the curve; default is the first line's" → rd_EP.

The fillet response reports the tangent points, delta, tangent length, and arc length.

One concern: the fillet trims lines at the tangent points — the arc is tangent to the lines at those points, same numerical issue as before, but fillet is a standard command and handles this properly.

Let's do fillet(ids: ["LN-003", "LN-004"], radius: 50). Both lines are on rd_EP, so the curve will also be placed on rd_EP.

Then verify: get_entity on the new arc, the lengths of LN-003/LN-004, and render_model to check visually.

Also let's confirm that the intersection is at [5000,5000], i.e., that the stationing is as the task states (not strictly necessary, but a quick check with list_alignments or station_to_xy… actually, the task already tells us the geometry, and the model confirms it: LN-001 y=5000 (MAIN's centerline), LN-002 x=5000 (CROSS's centerline), intersection [5000,5000]. Curb faces: MAIN ±44 → y=5044/4956; CROSS ±32 → x=5032/4968. The NE corner is at (5032, 5044). All consistent.)

Let's also confirm the other three corners are as I read: AR-001 SE (center 5082,4906), AR-002 SW (4918,4906), AR-003 NW (4918,5094). Yes, the NE is missing — consistent with the task.

Proceeding with the fillet.

- **LN-003** (MAIN ST north curb) trimmed back from the corner: now runs **[5082, 5044] → [5800, 5044]** (was 5032→5800).
- **LN-004** (CROSS AVE east curb) trimmed back from the corner: now runs **[5032, 5094] → [5032, 5700]** (was 5044→5700).
- Both curb lines kept their design anchors (station 18+82 @ 44 / 27+94 @ 32) and were re-stationed by the trim.

**2. Tool calls that mattered, in order**

1. `get_document_state` + `list_layers` — confirmed alignments, rd_EP layer, and that the design is local (not referenced).
2. `get_model_state` — identified the two un-filleted curb lines: **LN-003** (MAIN ST's 44 ft north face, y=5044, running east from 5032) and **LN-004** (CROSS AVE's 32 ft east face, x=5032, running north from 5044), meeting at the NE corner point (5032, 5044); confirmed the existing SE/SW/NW returns (AR-001/002/003) were all R=50.
3. `fillet` — `ids: ["LN-003", "LN-004"], radius: 50` → created AR-004 and auto-trimmed both lines to the tangent points (default keep = the far ends, which is correct since both lines run outward from the corner).
4. `get_entity` on AR-004, LN-003, LN-004 — verified arc geometry (center 5082,5094; angles 180°→270° CCW) and trim results.
5. `render_model` on the intersection window — final visual check.

**3. Failures, confusion, or manual math**

- No failures or error messages; the fillet reported on the first try: *"fillet AR-004 R=50.00' between LN-003 and LN-004: tangent points [5082.00, 5044.00] and [5032.00, 5094.00], Δ=90°00'00\", T=50.00', L=78.54', corner (PI) [5032.00, 5044.00]"*.
- No hand-computed coordinates were needed — the engine computed the tangent points. (Sanity check only: at a 90° corner with T=R=50, the center sits 50 ft in from each face, i.e. (5032+50, 5044+50) = (5082, 5094), and the tangent points fall 50 ft along each face — matching the engine's output and the established pattern of the other three returns, whose centers are 50 ft in from their corners too.)
